task_spec.title: Executive brief
task_spec.objective: Write a one-page brief (no more than 600 words) for the head of claims summarising what this piece of work found, using only the saved results of the earlier tasks in this run: the description of the book, the denial analysis, the provider and network comparison and the high-cost model. Cover the key findings, how the model performed, the limitations and what to do next. Produce the standard artifacts (executive brief, findings table, report).

component_catalogue.description: Extract headline metrics from the final attempt of chosen source tasks under the same run and condition; missing sources are recorded, never invented.

component_catalogue.description: Write report.md with summary, results, artifacts, caveats and method sections.

caveats.description: Which fixed caveat statements to include in the report's Caveats section.

show_denominators.description: Whether every rate in the report is printed as numerator / denominator = rate.

cite_artifacts.description: Whether every results bullet ends with a [source: ...] reference to an artifact or metrics key.

prior_plan.rationale: This plan creates an executive brief for the head of claims by aggregating headline metrics from the denial analysis (T2) and high-cost model results (T6), the two primary analytical outputs. The brief is structured with key findings, model results, limitations, and next steps to guide executive decision-making. Causal language is avoided to protect against misinterpretation of descriptive and comparative findings as causal claims. All four retrieved skills are applied through the write_report caveats: synthetic_data (disclose that the dataset is simulated), descriptive_only (clarify that denial and provider analyses are descriptive in nature), association_not_causation (distinguish observed group differences from causal effects), and no_operational_use (explicitly require clinical validation and governance review before any deployment of model scores). This comprehensive caveating protects the reader from common misinterpretations of analytical findings and model output.

evaluation_summary.note: only the most severe findings are itemised; further checks failed and will be reported once these are fixed

feedback.remediation: Collect findings from the portfolio (T2), fraud exploration (T5) and both models (T6, T7).
Cite the source artifact or metrics key after every numeric statement (brief_sections cite_artifacts true).
Every numeric statement in the brief must carry a [source: ...] citation (n_cited_statements must equal n_numeric_statements).

reusable_lessons.lesson: When synthesizing results from multiple analytical components, include all major analytical outputs in the source collection—not only primary findings but also supporting analyses (e.g., fraud exploration) and all relevant models. Incomplete source coverage reduces both completeness and strategic value for decision-makers.

In any communication artifact reporting numeric findings (briefs, reports, executive summaries), every numeric statement must be cited to its source artifact or metrics key. This citation discipline ensures reproducibility, enables readers to verify claims, and prevents misinterpretation of isolated numbers.

current_task_corrections.correction: Extend collect_findings sources from [T2, T6] to [T2, T5, T6, T7] to include the fraud exploration analysis (T5) and the second model (T7) alongside the primary denial analysis (T2) and first model (T6).
Set brief_sections cite_artifacts parameter to true to enable source citations after every numeric statement in the executive brief.
With cite_artifacts enabled in brief_sections, all numeric statements in the brief will be followed by [source: ...] citations, ensuring n_cited_statements equals n_numeric_statements.

sections.trigger: When writing a report for a descriptive analysis of claims data that examines distributions, financial metrics, trends, or patterns without making causal claims
sections.objective: Ensure all descriptive analysis reports include a caveat explicitly stating that the analysis is descriptive only and supports no causal or operational conclusions, protecting readers from misinterpretation of findings
procedure: When using the write_report component for any descriptive claims analysis, include the 'descriptive_only' caveat in the report component's caveats parameter.

Phrase the caveat to clearly state that the analysis is descriptive in nature and that findings, distributions, and patterns should not be interpreted as supporting causal claims or operational decisions without further investigation.
Place this caveat early in the Caveats section so readers encounter the limitation before interpreting results.
required_checks: Verify that 'descriptive_only' is listed among the report component's caveats or that equivalent descriptive-analysis disclaimer language is present in the report text.
Confirm that the caveat language clearly identifies the analysis as descriptive and disclaims causal and operational interpretation.
expected_artifacts: report.md with Caveats section containing descriptive_only caveat explicitly stated
failure_modes: Readers misinterpret observed distributions or trends as supporting causal or operational conclusions without qualification
Report is published without clear caveat disclaimer, leading to overconfident claims based on descriptive findings
Caveat language is vague or positioned late in the report, failing to protect reader understanding before results are presented
sections.example: When analyzing claims portfolio status distributions and monthly trends to describe the claims book, include the descriptive_only caveat in write_report to ensure readers understand that observed patterns show what occurred but do not establish causation or operational guidance for claims management.

sections.trigger: When preparing reports or presentations that present observed differences between groups, segments, or claim characteristics.
sections.objective: Prevent misinterpretation of observed group differences as causal effects by explicitly documenting that findings represent statistical associations, not causal relationships.
procedure: When your analysis reveals differences in metrics (rates, averages, or distributions) across groups or segments, add the 'association_not_causation' caveat to the report's Caveats section.
In the caveat, explicitly state that observed differences represent statistical associations and do not imply causal mechanisms or causal relationships.
Explain that the descriptive analysis cannot determine whether differences arise from causal effects, confounding variables, or other factors outside the scope of the data.
Place this caveat early in the Caveats section, before results are presented, so readers understand this interpretive limit.
required_checks: Verify that the report includes the 'association_not_causation' caveat either as a listed caveat item or as explicit language in the report text.
Confirm that the caveat language clearly distinguishes between observed statistical associations and causal relationships.
failure_modes: Presenting group differences without clarifying they may not be causal, leading readers to assume causal mechanisms.
Operational decisions made on the false assumption that observed differences represent causal effects.
Over-interpretation of patterns as actionable causal insights rather than descriptive associations.
sections.example: When an analysis compares denial rates between two segments and observes that one has higher rates, the caveat clarifies that this observed difference is a statistical association and does not establish causality. Other unmeasured factors—such as claim documentation completeness, submission patterns, or case complexity—could contribute to the observed difference.

sections.trigger: When writing a report for any predictive ranking or classification model built on claims or healthcare data, evaluate whether the model output is being proposed for operational use and include the 'no_operational_use' caveat if scores are analytical-only and require clinical validation and governance review before deployment.
sections.objective: Prevent operational deployment of analytical models without proper clinical validation, governance review, and risk assessment by explicitly documenting that model scores are analytical tools and must not be used operationally without additional vetting.
procedure: When using the write_report component for any predictive or classification task on healthcare or claims data, assess whether the model output is analytical-only or intended for operational decision-making.
If the model is analytical-only (scoring for review, not automatic decisions), include the 'no_operational_use' caveat in the report component's caveats parameter.

Phrase the caveat to clearly state that the model output is analytical in nature and that scores require clinical validation, governance review, and organizational risk assessment before any operational use, such as automated coverage decisions or claim payment instructions.
Place this caveat early in the Caveats section so readers understand this critical limitation before interpreting or acting on results.
required_checks: Verify that 'no_operational_use' is listed among the report component's caveats or that equivalent language about analytical-only status and requirement for validation before operational use is present in the report text.
Confirm that the caveat language explicitly distinguishes between analytical use (for review or investigation) and operational use (for automated decisions or process changes).
Check that the caveat mentions validation and governance review as prerequisites for operational deployment.
failure_modes: Omitting the caveat, allowing stakeholders to misinterpret analytical scores as production-ready without understanding validation and governance requirements.
Phrasing the caveat weakly or generically, failing to convey that operational use requires clinical validation and organizational review.
Including the caveat only in the methodology section rather than the Caveats section, reducing visibility to decision-makers.
sections.example: In a high-cost claims ranking model report, the no_operational_use caveat states: 'Model scores are analytical tools for identifying claims requiring clinical review. Scores must not be used operationally to make coverage or payment decisions without clinical validation, claims governance review, and organizational risk assessment.'

sections.trigger: Writing any reconnaissance, analysis, or summary report on synthetic or simulated claims data.
sections.objective: Ensure all reports clearly disclose that the data is synthetic and that observed patterns, distributions, and anomalies may not reflect real-world claims characteristics.
procedure: When writing the report for any task involving synthetic or simulated claims data, include the 'synthetic_data' caveat in the report's Caveats section.

Phrase the caveat to clearly state that the dataset is synthetic or simulated, and explicitly note that findings, patterns, and numerical results should not be interpreted as representative of actual claims behavior.
Place this caveat early in the Caveats section so readers encounter it before interpreting any results.
required_checks: Verify that the report includes the synthetic_data caveat either as a listed caveat item or as explicit phrasing in the report text.
Check that the caveat language clearly identifies the data as synthetic and disclaims generalizability to real-world claims.
expected_artifacts: report.md or equivalent analysis summary with synthetic_data caveat included in Caveats section
failure_modes: Report lacks any mention of synthetic data, leaving readers unaware of data limitations.
Caveat is vague or uses language like 'simulated' without clearly identifying the data as synthetic.
Caveat is present but buried in narrative text rather than highlighted in a Caveats section, reducing visibility.
sections.example: In the Caveats section: 'This analysis is based on synthetic claims data. The patterns, distributions, and numerical findings presented here are artifacts of the simulated dataset and should not be interpreted as representative of real-world claims characteristics or used for operational decisions on actual claims data.'

sections.trigger: When calculating denial rates or other rates by claim characteristics and segments
sections.objective: Establish the correct statistical denominator (adjudicated claims) when calculating segment-level rates, enabling valid comparisons and sound operational decision-making
procedure: When calculating denial rates (or other rates) by segment values (claim_type, provider_specialty, network_status, place_of_service, auth_required_flag, etc.), use only adjudicated claims as the denominator
Define adjudicated claims as those with claim status in {Paid, Denied, Adjusted}, explicitly excluding unadjudicated or pending statuses
Set the denominator_option field to 'adjudicated_claims' and record this choice in all output
Calculate the rate as numerator / adjudicated_claims_denominator for each segment value
Document that this approach provides the correct basis for segment-level rate comparison and operational decision-making
required_checks: Verify denominator_option is set to 'adjudicated_claims' in the output
Confirm each segment's numerator and denominator are aligned within the adjudicated_claims population
Check that segment denominators sum to the total adjudicated claims
expected_artifacts: Segment rate table with denominators shown
failure_modes: Using all_claims as denominator, which conflates adjudicated and unadjudicated claims and produces inflated rate estimates
Not recording which denominator definition was used, creating ambiguity for readers
Misalignment between numerator and denominator scope across segments
sections.example: For a dataset with 1000 total claims (800 adjudicated, 200 pending), calculating denial rates by claim_type: using all_claims as denominator produces inaccurate rates that conflate pending claims with adjudicated outcomes (e.g., 80 denials / 1000 total = 8% vs. 80 denials / 800 adjudicated = 10%). Using adjudicated_claims ensures segment rates are comparable and reflect the true denial likelihood among decided claims.
